title: Knowledge Check 1: Lessons 1-2
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 1-2 of the ai-power-user series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Per the lesson, what is the key thing that separates a power user from a regular user?
options: The power user owns a piece of their recurring work: they design how it runs, can change it, and answer for it
The power user has a faster or more expensive AI tool subscription
The power user never needs to check AI output before sending it
The power user uses AI for every single task, no exceptions
questions.explanation: The lesson's core line is about ownership, not skill: a power user takes a slice of their own recurring work, designs how it should run, keeps it changeable, and stays accountable for the output.

questions.question: Which of the three parts of owning a workflow involves staying accountable for the result that leaves your hands?
options: Designing the flow and choosing the order of steps
Keeping the setup editable so you can repair it when a tool changes
Answering for the output, because the human decides even when the tool drafts
Automating every repetitive task regardless of risk
questions.explanation: Ownership has three parts: design, change, and answer. The answer part is accountability, which the lesson ties to human-in-the-loop: the tool drafts, the human decides what ships.

questions.question: According to the lesson's Pareto framing, where should you point your workflow-building effort first?
options: At the largest or most interesting task, regardless of how often it happens
At the repetitive slice of your work, the roughly 20 percent of tasks with the same shape every time that carry most of the effort
At any task a colleague happens to mention, starting today
At the newest tool feature, to stay current
questions.explanation: The lesson uses the 80/20 rule to aim effort at the small slice of recurring, same-shape tasks, since that is where building a workflow pays for itself fastest.

questions.question: Per the lesson, why does an audit beat guessing from memory about how you spend your week?
options: Because memory flatters: you overestimate engaging or urgent tasks and underestimate quiet, repetitive ones, so an audit measures the week as it actually ran
Because an audit is faster than thinking about your work
Because memory is always wrong about everything, so any measurement is better
Because an audit tells you which tasks to stop doing entirely
questions.explanation: The lesson says your intuition is systematically wrong in one direction: you overestimate engaging or urgent tasks and underestimate quiet, repetitive ones. The audit corrects that by measuring the week as it actually ran.

questions.question: In the audit's three passes, what does pass three flag as a candidate for automation?
options: The tasks that have the same shape every time: the same inputs, the same steps, and the same output format
The largest or most visible task, regardless of how often it happens
The tasks that change shape each run and need your judgment
Any task a colleague mentions, starting today
questions.explanation: Pass three flags tasks with the same shape every time, the same inputs, steps, and output format. These are where a saved setup pays for itself, because every repetition after the first is cheaper.

questions.question: According to the lesson, which combination makes a task the ideal first candidate for a workflow?
options: Frequent, same-shaped, and low-risk to get wrong
Large, impressive, and done once a quarter
Rare, complex, and high-stakes so it gets attention
Irregular, judgment-heavy, and urgent
questions.explanation: The lesson names three tests: it is frequent, it is same-shaped, and it is low-risk to get wrong. A task meeting all three is the ideal first candidate, because the setup pays off and you can trust the workflow to draft while you decide.
